or grab a tool (R, D, O, A) and sketch by hand. Save keeps it on GitHub.

2 - Tests and Evals
- Run test to make sure that everything still works correctly. LLM to diagnose unit test that fails. This is to gate what's coming in or not. If test fails, not going in.
- Evals to make sure that everything still performs as expected. Not a quality gate. 

1.  how tests are run, not just from the system perspective, but also from a point of view of end-to-end agentic testing i.e. writing test cases, executing them, collecting data and results, diagnosing and reporting to engineers. This is something that's being actively worked on.
- [ALEX:] KNOWING WHAT THE CORRECT BEHAVIOR IS, AND THEN TO PRODUCE A TEST WORKFLOW TO VERIFY THAT BEHAVIOR.

- Agents write test, diagnose, and report.
- 
1) Choosing what to test:
- Triggers:
    - Changed lines with no coverage test. (new code)
    - Bug report. (Reproduce a known failure and diagnose)
    - Nightly runs, background sweep of risky code (Nightly diagnosis comes out with a file with low coverage, changed a lot in the last 7 days, linked to 5 recent incidents)
    - Bug that reached production uncaught. (a bug only fails with much much larger scale - production 10k users instead of 10 users)

- Responsibility for each component:
    - Impact Analyzer (Code) - produce the impact report by computing the build dependency delta (which targets changed, which dependency edges were added or removed, and which test depends on what changed -- which tests could be affected) and the code coverage delta (what changed lines are actually executed by tests -- which changed lines are actually tested)

    - The coverage gate (code) - this will read the report from the impact analyzer and decides if the code can be merged based on the statistics produced (how many tests passed, how many if else execution branches were covered).

    - Agent to review dependency: "Is this code good/necessary to add? If add and fails, who handle?"
        + Internal dependencies:
            * helper functions in own code base: Trivial if own code base (accept)
            * libraries from another team: Is this public API or private functionality? Accept if it's public API (getter/setter), reject if it's reaching the internals (something like private helpers, data models, database. If these break, the team who maintain these won't know who use it).
        + If there are new dependencies to external libraries, which can introduce cost and risk questions, license, security vulnerabilities, maintenance, and if we really need it due to all of those reason.
            * How big is the usage? Can it be replaced by an internal function? If yes, reject. If not, accept, and make sure to link metadata to our binary build.
        + Decide if it should accept, push back or ask human. This will be via another report with a suggested fix should anything is rejected.


    - Planner agent (Coding agent) - Read the report, see which gap needs to be addressed, which can be skipped, which has to be escalated to human.
        + address when there is a new or changed behavior; money, security, data is involved, a code is a known incident hotspot; new dependency or service edge appears, especially with external service; or clear expected outcome that can be tested.
        + skip when just symbol name change, unreachable code, logging or trivial getter, or known precedents that has a clear bypass.
        + remove overlaps between functional and code coverage before writing the actual test.
        + escalate to human when the expected behavior is unclear.
        + Output: CSV of {ID, expected behavior in plain english, expected outcome, test today (none/partial/name of test if covered), status (gap/covered/need human)}. Store this output in the database, keyed by target. Next time if a new PR that touches the target can check against this, and the background sweep can say this code has n behaviors, m tested, m/n %.
        + Group similar behaviors to task, assign to either functional writers or code coverage writers, or human accordingly, with human readable instructions explained in the notes.
        + IMPORTANT: ITS IMPORTANT TO KEEP TRACK OF THE TEST SO WE DONT KEEP REPEATING TESTS.

    
- Writing testcase:
    - Planner agents spin up (writer) sub agents, each one is doing a task (a group of behaviors). Make sure that the sub agents have their own independent context, own set of behaviors to cover so we don't do repeated work.

- Executing test: the Test Writer Agent writes the smallest number of tests where each one catches a different possible bug, usually 1–5 per task, and the Test Gate discards any that don't add new protection.
[EXPLANATION:]
    - Unchanged components: Scheduler, sandboxes, sharding, queues, retries
    - Changed with Agentic architecture:
        + Execution becomes an API instead of a pipeline stage Agent call test.run(workspace, targets, flags) via tool calling. This will let us run test in a loop (write -> run test -> read failures -> fix > run) instead of fixed, one pass pipeline (push code -> build -> test -> fail -> done).
                + An unit for an execution is a workspace which contains the commit being tested and anything that the agent produces (tests, fixes, test outputs). Test Writer Agent will write just enough tests to cover all the behaviors. The Test Gate (code) will run the candidate tests 20 times to make sure that they aren't flakey or filler tests (The tests that don't catch a deliberate bug that the Test Gate plant).

- collecting data and results:
    - workers upload output to the blob store, and the result service parses the output into result table.
    - Test database contains the Id of the test run, result, duration, the commit, the tool call in json, the S3 link to all the artifacts.
    - This history will be kept for book keeping purposes, such as identify flaky tests, grouping failures by signature, pass the diagnose to the Diagnosis agent instead of raw logs.


- Diagnosing:
    - Filter out results that are flaky tests, known failures, infra/versioning etc errors.
    - If it's one change that breaks (merged PR as a trigger), the agent reads the error and the stack trace and backtrack, find the exact error. And spin up a fixer agent to suggest the fix.
    - One agent to triage a cluster of changes. 50 changes merged today, all green yesterday, 20 broke just now. Whose change?
        + Bisect and find the change that breaks the tests, revert to see if it passes every test, and notify the owner of the change. 
        + We have the Action Cache and the workspace, which makes this action a lot cheaper. Those 50 changes probably touch 20-30 files, and the Action Cache lets us look up the command, the input files, and the corresponding binary. We can reuse a lot of the binaries between build with 25 changes and build with 12 changes or 37 changes. Agent works in the workspace, so basically 1 docker image to test the changes until it finds the culprit. This means 1) humans don't have to do it 2) when agent finds the change, it notifies the only person whose change breaks nightly test instead of everyone else.
    - Obviously this agent will also look up the history in the test DB and see if the behavior is classified as flaky or known behaviors as mentioned in the collecting data and results section












5. Scaling the test runners is also a problem. There are various levels of tests (this is important). Lets say level-1 block build and fail it and run for each build. Level-2 runs every 4 hours or everyday.  Level-3 takes your nightly build and deploys onto test hardware and runs bigger tests. This layered approach is preferred, and you can mention it. Usually, the agentic testing, imo, will help more in level-2 and level-3.


6. I think optimization, in this interview, can be covered at a high level, just be sure to understand if it generates like a lot of candidate optimization ideas, do you need human review? Because running useless optimization approaches on each fork, might eat up capacity.


7. evals for model(s) you'll use for optimization will also be important. I think its not just optimizing the code, because you can run models on build data to suggest build time optimization (my VP loves this).
